extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and policymakers interested in peer review and scholarly-publishing innovation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and designing peer review models and practices (anonymity, openness, decoupling, pre/post-publication review, reputation/incentives) for scholarly publishing. The focus is on trade-offs, empirical evidence, and operational features for implementing novel peer review systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing review reports publicly (open reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility of publishing the reviews online has been associated with a high decline rate among potential peer reviewers, and an increase in the amount of time taken to write a review, but with no effect on review quality (van Rooyen et al., 2010). This suggests that the barriers to publishing review reports are inherently social, rather than technical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider social effects (reviewer willingness to accept invitations, time cost) vs technical feasibility. Unresolved issues include whether reports should be posted for ultimately unpublished manuscripts, the impact of author identification/anonymity, and the potential career-stage consequences. Also consider readership and real-world usage of published reports; benefits may be long-term and hard to measure immediately. Different reviewer populations will have varying perspectives; no single policy likely fits all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of anonymity (single/double/triple blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different levels of bi-directional anonymity occur in peer review (single blind, double blind, triple blind). Traditional double blind review is based on the idea that peer evaluations should be impartial and based on the research, not ad hominem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh theoretical impartiality benefits against practical difficulties in protecting anonymity (language, prior knowledge, conference presentations, web searches). Triple-blind extends anonymity to handling editors. Evidence on effects is mixed: some studies show improved quality with blinding; others find no effect. Consider discipline-specific feasibility and the risk that anonymity may enable more aggressive or negligent reviewer behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signed (eponymous) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Signed peer review (reviewer names revealed) aims to encourage civility, accountability, and more thoughtful reviews, and to extend review into an ongoing community dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: increased civility, accountability, potential for validation and community dialogue; evidence shows signed reviews can be more courteous, higher quality, and take longer. Risks: may reduce criticalness, introduce skew and bias via community selectivity, create one-sided accountability (reviewers exposed while authors protected), discourage junior reviewers from being candid for fear of retaliation. Consider safeguards (e.g., COPE guidance, dispute-resolution mechanisms) and cultural differences across communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of identification/anonymity on reviewer behavior and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Revealing reviewer identity may lower the likelihood of accepting review invitations, may make signed reviews more polite and more likely to recommend acceptance, and has mixed effects on review quality based on randomized and observational studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate empirical evidence: some trials showed blinding improved review quality, others found no effect. Consider metrics such as acceptance rate to review invitations, time to complete reviews, politeness/tone, and recommendation patterns. Be cautious interpreting heterogeneous study results and discipline differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of early-career and marginalized researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity can protect junior researchers and other marginalized demographics from retaliatory backlashes if they write critical reviews; signed reviews may deter such reviewers from participating or being candid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for differential risk across career stages and communities. Before implementing transparency measures, engage carefully with high-risk or marginalized groups and design protections (e.g., confidential reporting, ODR/COPE-informed mechanisms) to mitigate potential harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ethics and dispute-resolution frameworks (COPE/ODR)
rubrics_metrics.description: COPE provides advice to editors and publishers on publication ethics and handling misconduct, and Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) experience can be used to prevent, mitigate, and deal with misconduct during peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt formal mechanisms adapted to innovative peer review models: use COPE guidelines for publication ethics and consider integrating ODR-style processes for dispute handling in open or identified review systems to address alleged misconduct or retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic bias monitoring and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is intrinsically biased across social dimensions (gender, institution prestige, nationality, language). Studies show systemic bias (e.g., against women and authors from less prestigious institutions) is embedded in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any peer review policy should account for systemic biases. Avoid single blanket policies; instead favour flexible, customizable policies tailored to different research communities. Monitor acceptance rates, reviewer/editor gender and institution effects, and implement interventions (e.g., double-blind where feasible) where evidence suggests bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoupling peer review from publishing (publish-then-filter / post-publication review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoupling separates journal functions (archiving, registration, dissemination) from peer review/certification. Post-publication peer review means filtering and evaluation occur after initial communication of research (publish then filter). Platforms include RIO, PubPub, ScienceOpen, The Winnower, F1000 Research and annotation services like hypothes.is, PaperHive, PubPeer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess pre-submission vs post-publication workflows, platform interoperability, discoverability of post-publication evaluations, incentives for engagement, and cultural acceptance. Consider whether platforms accept and forward reviews to journals and how costs, portability (MECA), and editorial practices interact with traditional journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portable/portable review and platform-mediated pre-submission review
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms (Peerage of Science, RUBRIQ, Axios Review) allow authors to submit to platforms for review first; platforms provide referees and forward manuscripts and reports to journals. MECA (Manuscript Exchange Common Approach) aims to provide portable review exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cost models (sometimes deductible from publication fees), journal acceptance of platform reviews, potential to reduce redundancy and editorial workload, and maturity/viability (many initiatives are nascent or have closed due to low uptake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-prints and overlay journal models
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-print servers (arXiv, bioRxiv) enable initial publication prior to journal peer review; overlay journals perform peer review as an additional layer on top of pre-prints, leaving content on pre-print servers and listing peer-reviewed versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider field-specific uptake (strong in physics/math, slower in other fields), reputation/stigma issues, citation patterns, and whether overlay journals or platform-integrated models (PubPub, EPISCIENCES, ScienceOpen) can scale beyond niche domains. Evaluate costs (generally cheap/rapid) and discoverability of peer-reviewed versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage peer review / Registered Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered Reports split peer review into two stages: (1) review of research questions and methodology prior to data collection, with provisional acceptance if high-quality; (2) post-study review confirming results and adherence to the originally described methodology. Designed to boost research integrity and reduce publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Stage 1 to evaluate study design, power, and methods; provisional acceptance removes incentives for selective reporting. Stage 2 confirms adherence and soundness of results. Benefits: reduces p-hacking, HARKing, low statistical power; incentivizes data-sharing and accurate reporting. Suitable for hypothesis-driven research; journals and communities must adopt and operationalize the two-stage workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer Review by Endorsement (author-guided pre-publication review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors solicit reviews from peers prior to submission; endorsements/reviewer identities are made public alongside manuscripts (ScienceOpen PRE, RIO). Functionally similar to contributed submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: faster, cheaper, potentially less editorial gatekeeping; may help non-native English speakers work with reviewers/editors in their first languages. Risks: potential bias from author-selected reviewers—mitigated by public disclosure of identities and endorsements. Consider transparency of endorsements and community trust mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiparametric community-evaluation platforms (e.g., LIBRE/Open Scholar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repositories/platforms can combine reviewers’ assessments, citation indices, community ratings, and usage statistics to calculate multiparametric performance metrics and allow authors to upload improved versions or submit to journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design performance metrics carefully (which signals to reward), ensure community-based evaluation is discoverable and interoperable, and provide clear pathways for versioning and journal submission. Monitor for gaming and ensure proper recognition and attribution (ORCID, CrossRef, Creative Commons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability, aggregation, and interoperability of post-publication evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many post-publication services are non-interoperable; evaluations are difficult to discover, lost, or rarely available in context for re-use, hindering recognition as a valuable community process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize aggregation and interoperability (indexing, APIs, common metadata) so post-publication reviews and annotations are discoverable and usable by readers, institutions, and aggregators. Without this, low engagement and limited impact are likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical mass, community uptake, and cultural inertia
rubrics_metrics.description: A critical mass of researcher uptake is required for peer-to-peer reputation/evaluation systems to succeed; cultural inertia in researcher workflows strongly inhibits uptake of new models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance incentives and ease-of-use to reduce friction. Recognize differing motivations across scholarly communities; incrementally adapt successful features from popular social/web applications. Expect slow adoption without clear incentives, evidence of benefit, and alignment with existing workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key features for next-generation peer review platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Any future peer review platform would benefit from: 1) Quality control and moderation, possibly through openness and transparency; 2) Certification via personalized reputation or performance metrics; 3) Incentive structures to motivate and encourage engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design platforms to combine robust moderation (to maintain quality and civility), trusted certification mechanisms (reputation metrics, verified endorsements), and incentives (credit, recognition, rewards) tuned to the target research communities to overcome low uptake and ensure sustainable engagement.
